statement: The input is the bytes before its first NUL byte; anything after it is ignored.
A backslash followed by `n` (0x6E) becomes one newline byte (0x0A).
A backslash followed by any byte other than `n` becomes one backslash, and that byte is dropped. In particular `\\` becomes `\`, `\t` becomes `\` and `\N` becomes `\`.
A backslash that is the last byte of the input stays a backslash.
Every byte that is not part of an escape is copied unchanged, including control bytes and bytes 0x80 to 0xFF.
Escapes do not chain: the input is scanned once, left to right, and the output is never re-scanned. `\\n` becomes `\n` (two bytes, backslash and `n`).
The output is never longer than the input.

Command-line options are matched against the arguments after the program name, exactly and case-sensitively (`Q_strcmp`), and the first occurrence wins. An option that takes a value (`-basedir`, `-game`, `-cachedir`) is ignored when it is the last argument.

The base directory is the argument after `-basedir` if there is one; otherwise the host's default, which is the current working directory on Windows (`sys_win.c`) and DOS (`sys_dos.c`) and `.` on Linux (`sys_linux.c`).

If the base directory ends with `/` or `\`, exactly one such character is removed; any others stay. `-basedir ..//base//` gives the game directory `..//base//id1`. An empty base directory stays empty, giving `/id1`.

Adding a game directory `D` puts `D` at the head of the search path, then for N = 0, 1, 2, ... puts the archive `D/pakN.pak` (N in decimal, no padding) at the head, stopping at the first N whose file cannot be opened. The result, from the head, is `D/pakK.pak`, ..., `D/pak1.pak`, `D/pak0.pak`, `D`: a game directory's archives are searched before its loose files, and higher-numbered archives before lower ones.

The archive scan stops at the first missing number: with `pak0.pak` and `pak2.pak` but no `pak1.pak`, `pak2.pak` is never loaded. With no `pak0.pak` the game directory has only its loose files. A missing archive is not an error, and neither is a missing game directory.
An archive that opens but fails to load (PAK-1, PAK-2) is fatal; it is not skipped.

Game directories are added in this order, each in front of the previous ones: `<base>/id1` always; `<base>/rogue` if `-rogue` is given; `<base>/hipnotic` if `-hipnotic` is given; `<base>/<value>` if `-game <value>` is given. The order does not depend on the order of the options on the command line, so with both `-rogue` and `-hipnotic`, `hipnotic` is searched before `rogue`.

The value of `-game` is appended to `<base>/` as given: it is not checked, and it may contain `/` or `..`. `-game` marks the game as modified (FS-4.3). `-game id1` adds `id1` a second time, which changes no lookup result.
The game directory the engine writes to (`com_gamedir`, used by `COM_WriteFile`) is the last directory added by FS-1.7.

`-path` discards the search path built by FS-1 and builds a new one from the arguments that follow it, up to the end or the first argument starting with `+` or `-`. Each is put at the head in turn, so the last one listed is searched first. `-path` with no such argument leaves the search path empty. It does not change the game directory of FS-1.9, and it marks the game as modified (FS-4.3).

A `-path` argument whose extension (FS-2.3) is exactly `pak` is loaded as an archive; if it cannot be opened, the engine stops with the fatal error `Couldn't load packfile: <argument>`. Any other argument is a directory, and it is not checked to exist.

A `-path` argument's extension is the text after the first `.` anywhere in it, at most 7 bytes, compared case-sensitively. So `mod/pak0.pak` is an archive, but `./id1/pak0.pak` (extension `/id1/pa`) and `id1/PAK1.PAK` (extension `PAK`) are directories.
With `-proghack`, a lookup of exactly `progs.dat` starts at the second element of the search path instead of the first. No other name is affected.

QuakeC Studio does not implement `-cachedir` (a deliberate divergence). In id's engine it copies loose files from the search path into a local cache directory and reads the copy; it is off unless asked for on every platform (`sys_win.c` sets `parms.cachedir = NULL`, and `sys_linux.c` has "caching is disabled by default, use -cachedir to enable"), and it exists to speed up installs on network drives, which is not a property of game data.
A lookup returns the file from the first element of the search path, from the head, that has it. Elements after that one are not consulted, and nothing is merged across elements.
An archive element has a name if one of its entries matches by PAK-3.1.
A directory element has a name if the file `<directory>/<name>` exists and can be opened for reading. The name is joined with a single `/` and not otherwise changed.

In the shareware game (FS-4.2), directory elements are skipped for any name that contains `/` or `\`; archive elements are not affected. A loose `progs.dat` is still found; a loose `maps/start.bsp` is not.
A name found nowhere is not an error at this level: the lookup reports no file, and the caller decides (`COM_LoadFile` returns `NULL`).

A found file's size is the entry's `filelen` for an archive, or the file's length for a directory. `COM_LoadFile` returns its bytes followed by one NUL byte that is not counted in the size, so text files can be parsed as C strings.

Names in directory elements, the archive names of FS-1.4 and the game directory names of FS-1.7 are matched ASCII case-insensitively on every OS. id's code leaves this to the host filesystem, so the answer differs by platform; this spec fixes the answer of the DOS and Windows reference builds, whose filesystems ignore case, so that an install copied from a CD (`ID1/PAK0.PAK`) or a mod made on Windows behaves the same on macOS and Linux. Archive entries stay case-sensitive (PAK-3.1).

A name that is absolute (starts with `/` or `\`, or a drive letter and `:`), or that has a `..` path component, never matches a directory element (a deliberate divergence). id's code joins it unchanged, so it can read files outside the game directory; QuakeC Studio confines reads to the install. Such a name still matches an archive entry with exactly that name (PAK-3.1).

QuakeC Studio puts no limit on path lengths (a deliberate divergence). id's engine builds search-path and archive paths in `MAX_OSPATH` (128-byte) buffers with `strcpy` and `sprintf`, which overflow, undefined, when the joined path is longer; the length depends on where the player installed the game, not on the game data.

QuakeC Studio puts no limit on the number of archives (a deliberate divergence). On Windows, id's engine has `MAX_HANDLES` 10 file handles, of which `findhandle` uses slots 1 to 9; every loaded archive holds one for the whole session, and running out is the fatal error `out of handles`. That is a limit of one host's file layer, not of the format.
Once the search path is built, the engine looks up `gfx/pop.lmp` by FS-3, with the shareware restriction of FS-3.4 off, so a loose `id1/gfx/pop.lmp` counts.

If `gfx/pop.lmp` is not found, the game is shareware. If it is found, its first 256 bytes, read as 128 big-endian 16-bit values, must equal the 128 values of the `pop` table in `common.c`; if they do, the game is registered, and if they do not, the engine stops with the fatal error `Corrupted data file.`. A `gfx/pop.lmp` shorter than 256 bytes is the same error: id's code compares whatever the short read left in its uninitialised buffer, which is undefined, and this spec fixes the answer as the mismatch.
A shareware game that is marked as modified (by PAK-4.2, `-game` or `-path`) stops with the fatal error `You must have the registered version to use modified games`.
After the check, FS-3.4 applies to every lookup in a shareware game and to none in a registered one.

A rerelease install is a base directory of its own: on Steam it is the `rerelease` folder inside the original install, and elsewhere (GOG's Quake Enhanced, Epic, Game Pass) it is the game's install folder. Its `id1` holds `pak0.pak` and no `pak1.pak`.

The rerelease's game directories (`id1`, `hipnotic`, `rogue`, `dopa`, `mg1` and any others it ships) are searched by FS-1 and FS-3 unchanged, with the rerelease folder as the base directory and the expansion chosen by `-game`, as QuakeSpasm and vkQuake run them.

`QuakeEX.kpf` in the rerelease base directory is a zip archive (it holds the localization strings, such as `localization/loc_english.txt`, that the rerelease's progs and maps refer to). It is not an element of the search path: FS-3 never finds a file inside it.

QuakeC Studio does not model the KEX engine's per-user game directories (`Saved Games\Nightdive Studios\Quake`); the rerelease engine is a compile target only (ENG-8), and the search path is the one id's engine builds.
A PAK file starts with a 12-byte header: the four bytes `PACK` (0x50 0x41 0x43 0x4B), then `dirofs` and `dirlen` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.

If the first four bytes are not exactly `PACK` (the comparison is case-sensitive, so `pack` fails), loading fails with the error `<path> is not a packfile`. In id's engine this is a fatal `Sys_Error`.

A file of fewer than 12 bytes fails to load. id's code does not check the length of the read and decodes whatever was in the uninitialised header struct, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error, the same as PAK-1.2, because no valid archive is that short.
A PAK path that cannot be opened is not an error of the format: `COM_LoadPackFile` returns `NULL` and its caller decides what that means (FS-1.5, FS-2.2).
The directory is `dirlen` bytes at offset `dirofs`, holding 64-byte entries: a 56-byte name, then `filepos` and `filelen` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.
The number of entries is `dirlen` divided by 64, rounded down. The remaining `dirlen % 64` bytes are not an entry; they are still read, and they count towards the CRC of PAK-4.1.
A `dirlen` from 0 to 63 gives an archive with no entries, which loads without error.
More than 2048 entries fails with the error `<path> has <n> files` (fatal in id's engine), where `<n>` is the computed entry count. Exactly 2048 entries loads.

A negative `dirlen` fails as PAK-2.4. The engine divides `dirlen` as an unsigned 32-bit value on the reference build, so any negative `dirlen` gives at least 33,554,432 entries; `dirlen` = -64 gives `has 67108863 files`. (A 64-bit build gets a different, also failing, result; the 32-bit answer is the one fixed here.)

A `dirlen` from 131,073 to 131,135 (2048 whole entries plus part of another) fails to load. id's code computes 2048 entries, passes the limit check and then reads `dirlen` bytes into a 131,072-byte stack array, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error because the C overflows its buffer.

A directory that does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `dirofs`, or `dirofs + dirlen` past the end) fails to load. id's code does not check the seek or the length of the read and parses uninitialised stack memory, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
An entry's name is the bytes of its 56-byte field before the first NUL. Bytes after that NUL are ignored.

An entry whose 56-byte name field contains no NUL fails the load. id's `strcpy` runs on into `filepos`, `filelen` and the next entries, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error because no tool writes such a name and no single answer matches the C.

Names are kept as raw bytes: no case folding, no conversion between `/` and `\`, no trimming. `MAPS/E1M1.BSP` and `maps/e1m1.bsp` are two different names. An entry whose first name byte is NUL has the empty name.
Entries keep their directory order, and two entries may have the same name; loading neither merges nor rejects them.
`filepos` and `filelen` are not checked when the archive is loaded, so a bad range never stops an archive from loading or its directory from being listed (PAK-3.4 covers reading such an entry).
Looking up a name in an archive returns the first entry, in directory order, whose name is byte-for-byte equal to it. The comparison is case-sensitive and does not normalise separators.
An entry's contents are the `filelen` bytes starting at offset `filepos` of the PAK file. Entries may overlap each other, the header or the directory; nothing checks it.
An entry with `filelen` 0 has empty contents.

Reading an entry whose range does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `filepos` or `filelen`, or `filepos + filelen` past the end) is an error. id's code either fails in `Hunk_AllocName` (`Hunk_Alloc: bad size` for `filelen` below -1), writes before its buffer (`filelen` = -1) or returns the short read's uninitialised bytes; this spec fixes the answer as an error. The entry is still listed (PAK-2.12).

The directory CRC is CRC-16 with polynomial 0x1021, not reflected, initial value 0xFFFF and no final XOR, computed over all `dirlen` bytes of the directory as they are in the file (before byte swapping, and including any partial entry from PAK-2.2). The CRC of an empty directory is 0xFFFF (65535).

An archive whose entry count is not 339 or whose directory CRC is not 32981 marks the game as modified. The check runs on every archive loaded, not only `pak0.pak`, and it never stops an archive from loading.

The rerelease's `pak0.pak` archives (in `id1`, `hipnotic`, `rogue`, `dopa`, `mg1` and the other game directories of FS-5.2) are PAK archives as described by PAK-1 to PAK-3, each with at most 2048 entries, and need no extension of the format. This statement rests on QuakeSpasm's evidence above; it is confirmed against a real install by the reader's acceptance test in [#42](https://github.com/quakecstudio/editor/issues/42), because no rerelease data is available to CI (LIC-4).
A WAD2 file starts with a 12-byte header: the four bytes `WAD2` (0x57 0x41 0x44 0x32), then `numlumps` and `infotableofs` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers.

If the first four bytes are not exactly `WAD2`, loading fails with the error `Wad file <name> doesn't have WAD2 id` (fatal in id's engine). `wad.h` comments the field "should be WAD2 or 2DAW", but the code accepts only `WAD2`; `WAD3` and `2DAW` fail.
A file of fewer than 12 bytes fails to load. id's code reads the header from the loaded buffer without checking its length, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.
The engine finds `gfx.wad` through the game filesystem (FS-3), so a mod can replace it; if it is not found, the engine stops with the fatal error `W_LoadWadFile: couldn't load gfx.wad`.

The directory is `numlumps` 32-byte entries at offset `infotableofs`: `filepos`, `disksize` and `size` as signed 32-bit little-endian integers, then the `type` and `compression` bytes, two unused bytes and a 16-byte name.
`numlumps` 0 gives an archive with no lumps, which loads without error.

A negative `numlumps` fails to load. id's loop compares an unsigned counter with it, so it walks about four billion entries past the buffer, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

A directory that does not lie wholly inside the file (a negative `infotableofs`, or `infotableofs + 32 * numlumps` past the end) fails to load. id's code does not check it, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as an error.

Each lump name is cleaned when the archive loads (`W_CleanupName`): the bytes of the 16-byte field up to the first NUL are kept, ASCII `A` to `Z` become `a` to `z`, every other byte (including 0x80 to 0xFF) is unchanged, and the rest of the field is filled with NUL. The comment above `W_CleanupName` says it pads with spaces; the code pads with NUL. Bytes after the first NUL are discarded.
A 16-byte name field with no NUL keeps all 16 bytes as the name. id's `strcmp` on such a name reads past the field, which is undefined; this spec fixes the answer as a 16-byte name.

`type`, `compression` and `disksize` are not checked. The engine uses `type` only to byte-swap the width and height of `TYP_QPIC` (66) lumps, which changes nothing on little-endian hosts. `compression` is ignored: `CMP_LZSS` (1) is defined in `wad.h` but no WinQuake code decompresses a lump, so a lump's bytes are always returned as stored.
`filepos`, `disksize` and `size` are not checked when the archive loads, so a bad range never stops an archive from loading or its directory from being listed.
Lumps keep their directory order, and two lumps may have the same cleaned name.

A lookup cleans the requested name by the rule of WAD-2.5 and returns the first lump, in directory order, whose cleaned name equals it. Lookups therefore ignore ASCII case (`CoNcHaRs` finds `CONCHARS`) but not the case of bytes 0x80 to 0xFF.

Only the first 16 bytes of the requested name count. A requested name of 16 or more bytes is compared as its first 16 bytes; id's code compares an unterminated buffer there, which is undefined, and this spec fixes the answer by WAD-2.6.
A name that matches no lump is the error `W_GetLumpinfo: <name> not found` (fatal in id's engine).

A lump's data starts at `filepos`. QuakeC Studio reads a lump as the `disksize` bytes at `filepos` (the bytes stored in the file; the engine itself never needs a length), and reading a lump whose range does not lie wholly inside the file is an error. The lump is still listed (WAD-2.8).

Looking up a lump by index accepts 0 to `numlumps - 1`. id's `W_GetLumpNum` accepts `numlumps` too (its test is `num > wad_numlumps`), which reads one entry past the directory; this spec fixes `numlumps` as an error. `W_GetLumpNum` has no caller in WinQuake (GitHub code search of `id-Software/Quake`, 2026-10-16, finds it only in `wad.c` and `wad.h`).
A picture lump (`TYP_QPIC`) is a `width` and a `height`, signed 32-bit little-endian, followed by `width * height` bytes of palette indices, row by row from the top left.

The `conchars` lump has no header: it is 128 by 128 bytes of palette indices, 16 rows of 16 characters of 8 by 8 pixels, character `n` at row `n >> 4` and column `n & 15`, with index 0 drawn as transparent.

A texture lump (`TYP_MIPTEX`) starts with a `miptex_t`: a 16-byte name, then `width`, `height` and four mip offsets as unsigned 32-bit little-endian integers, the offsets from the start of the lump. id's engine never reads a texture lump from a WAD; the same structure in a BSP file is the BSP spec's, and WAD2 texture files are read only by map tools and editors.
